info.text: Quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: Which two points are enough to determine an axis-aligned rectangle?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The bottom-left corner holds the smallest x and y, and the top-right corner holds the largest. Together they fix all four edges.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: The bottom-left corner and the top-right corner
Any two points on its sides

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x1 = 2, y1 = 1, x2 = 7, y2 = 4;
int w = x2 - x1;
int h = y2 - y1;
cout << w << " " << h << " " << w * h << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The width is 7 - 2 = 5, the height is 4 - 1 = 3, and the area is 5 x 3 = 15.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: When are two axis-aligned rectangles separated horizontally?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Then there is no x value that belongs to both of them, so they cannot overlap whatever their heights are.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: When one of them ends at or before the start of the other on the x axis

What does this program print?

main.cpp
int a1 = 1, b1 = 2, a2 = 7, b2 = 6;

questiontext.text: Why do we use <= (and not <) when testing whether two rectangles are separated?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Rectangles that touch along an edge or at a corner share zero area. With <= they count as separated, which is the right answer.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: So that rectangles that only touch are not counted as overlapping

name.text: Q07 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct functions into the gaps so the program prints the shared width 2 of the strips [1,6] and [4,9].

main.cpp
int a1 = 1, a2 = 6, b1 = 4, b2 = 9;
int w = [[1]](a2, b2) - [[2]](a1, b1);
cout << w << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The shared part ends at the smaller end (min(6, 9) = 6) and starts at the larger start (max(1, 4) = 4), so its width is 2.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int a1 = 1, a2 = 6, b1 = 4, b2 = 9;
int w = min(a2, b2) - max(a1, b1);
cout << w << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

questiontext.text: Two posters have areas 15 and 9 and share an area of 6. How much wall do they cover together?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Adding the areas counts the shared part twice, so we subtract it once: 15 + 9 - 6 = 18.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Normalized rectangle  →  [[1]]

Intersection  →  [[2]]

Interval  →  [[3]]

Bounding box  →  [[4]]

Union area  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five words describe the whole lesson: how a rectangle is stored, and how two of them relate.

The correct answer:

  • Normalized rectangle → The first corner has the smaller coordinates
  • Intersection → The part shared by two shapes
  • Interval → A segment with a start and an end
  • Bounding box → The smallest rectangle containing all the points
  • Union area → Everything the two shapes cover together

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program prints 2.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. hi uses lo, so lo must come first. Then len uses both, and the print comes last. With lo = 5 and hi = 7 the length is 2.

The correct answer:

name.text: Q15 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operator into the gap so the program says that the strips [0,3] and [3,6], which only touch, are apart (it should print 1).

main.cpp
int a1 = 0, a2 = 3, b1 = 3, b2 = 6;
bool apart = a2 [[1]] b1 || b2 <= a1;
cout << apart << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. With a2 <= b1 we get 3 <= 3, which is true: touching strips share no length. With < the test would be false and the strips would wrongly look overlapped.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int a1 = 0, a2 = 3, b1 = 3, b2 = 6;
bool apart = a2 <= b1 || b2 <= a1;
cout << apart << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each expression with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

hi.x - lo.x  →  [[1]]

max(a.lo.x, b.lo.x)  →  [[2]]

min(a.hi.y, b.hi.y)  →  [[3]]

max(0, ...)  →  [[4]]

area(a) + area(b) - overlap  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Every formula in this lesson is built from these five pieces.

The correct answer:

  • hi.x - lo.x → The width of a rectangle
  • max(a.lo.x, b.lo.x) → The left edge of the intersection
  • min(a.hi.y, b.hi.y) → The top edge of the intersection
  • max(0, ...) → Turns a negative overlap into zero
  • area(a) + area(b) - overlap → The area the two rectangles cover

questiontext.text:
Sort each edge: is it computed with max or with min?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Left edge of an intersection  →  [[1]]

Bottom edge of an intersection  →  [[1]]

Right edge of a bounding box  →  [[1]]

Right edge of an intersection  →  [[2]]

Top edge of an intersection  →  [[2]]

Left edge of a bounding box  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. An intersection starts at the larger start and ends at the smaller end. A bounding box does the opposite: it starts at the smallest value and ends at the largest.

The correct answer:

max: Left edge of an intersection, Bottom edge of an intersection, Right edge of a bounding box
min: Right edge of an intersection, Top edge of an intersection, Left edge of a bounding box

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Its smallest and largest x are the same, and so are its y values, so the width and height are both 0.
